title: The interrobang
hook: In 1962 an ad man fused the question mark and exclamation mark into one.
peek: The interrobang, a question mark laid over an exclamation mark, was dreamed up by a New York advertising executive in 1962. It got its own typeface and even its own typewriter key before quietly fading away.
lede: Martin Speckter ran an advertising agency in New York and noticed that copywriters kept ending excited questions with a question mark and an exclamation mark side by side. He thought the pair looked untidy. In 1962, in a typography magazine he edited, he proposed a single mark that does both jobs at once: a question mark and an exclamation mark printed on top of each other.

bullets.text: Speckter asked readers for names, and suggestions included exclamaquest. He settled on interrobang, joining the Latin interrogatio, a question, with bang, old printers' slang for the exclamation mark.

In 1966 the American Type Founders typeface Americana became one of the first to include an interrobang. For a few years the mark was a minor fad, written up in newspapers and magazines across the United States.

By the late 1960s some Remington typewriters offered an interrobang key. The craze faded within a decade, but the mark survives in Unicode and in many modern fonts, ready for anyone who wants to ask a question and shout it at the same time.
